title: A low-cost compact muon detector for millikelvin operation
authors: Tengiz Ibrayev, Danish Khan, Alex Herscovics, Komal Kataruka, Matilda Lawton, Sandhya Sharma, Steven Waddy, Laura Manenti
abstract: Ionizing radiation produces correlated errors in superconducting qubits, posing some challenges to quantum error correction. In addition, it causes background events in other superconducting cryogenic devices, such as kinetic inductance detectors and superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors. Cosmic muons are a component of this background that can only be partly shielded against at ground level, but can be tagged by an independent detector inside the cryostat, so that the affected data can be vetoed, or the muon tags incorporated into error correction.   We present a low-cost, compact muon detector consisting of two plastic scintillator modules, each read out by a silicon photomultiplier (SiPM), operated in coincidence. We characterize the SiPMs from room temperature down to 10 mK, including the breakdown and upper-limit voltages that define the operating bias range. Operated as a muon counter, the detector measures a coincidence rate that, as expected, is independent of temperature within uncertainties and agrees with analytical and Monte Carlo predictions.   Below approximately 8 K, each muon event produces two pulses, one narrow and one broad, an effect that, to our knowledge, has not been reported before. Coincidences with an independent muon detector outside the cryostat confirm that muons are still counted reliably in this regime. By studying the appearance of double pulses as a function of temperature and magnetic field up to 4.5 T, we find a behavior consistent with the phase diagram of a type-II superconductor. This links the double pulses to a superconducting material in the SiPM, likely an adhesion layer or diffusion barrier introduced during manufacturing. The mechanism by which the superconducting state produces the second pulse is not yet understood.
summary: This paper presents a low-cost muon detector designed to veto background noise in superconducting quantum devices. By operating the detector down to millikelvin temperatures, the researchers observed a novel double-pulse signature. This signature's behavior strongly correlates with the phase diagram of a Type-II superconductor, suggesting a superconducting mechanism within the detector's readout electronics.
main_problem: Cosmic muons create background noise in superconducting cryogenic detectors, interfering with quantum measurements and requiring robust background tagging.
main_result: The detector exhibits an unexpected double-pulse signature below 8 K, whose behavior strongly suggests a superconducting transition within the SiPM material itself.
method: The authors constructed and characterized a compact muon detector using plastic scintillators read out by SiPMs, measuring coincidence rates and analyzing pulse shapes across millikelvin temperatures.
model_or_system: The system is a coincidence muon detector built around SiPMs, whose electrical response is analyzed by characterizing its breakdown voltage ($V_{BD}$) and upper-limit voltage ($V_{UL}$) as a function of temperature and magnetic field.
key_observables: Coincidence rate, double-pulse waveform characteristics (narrow/broad components), $V_{BD}(T)$, and $V_{UL}(T)$.
important_parameters: Temperature range (up to 10 mK), Magnetic field (up to 4.5 T), Transition temperature ($T_c \approx 8.08$ K).
main_assumptions: The double pulse generation is attributed to the sensor response to light interacting with a superconducting material within the SiPM, rather than readout electronics.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate SiPM I-V curves, the experimental setup for muon rate measurements, and plots showing the temperature and magnetic field dependence of the double-pulse signature.
paper_structure: The paper first addresses the problem of muon background in quantum devices, then details the detector construction and SiPM characterization across cryogenic temperatures, culminating in the observation and analysis of the temperature-dependent double-pulse phenomenon.
why_interesting: The study provides an experimental link between high-energy particle detection (muons) and fundamental condensed matter phenomena (superconductivity) in a highly sensitive quantum measurement platform (SiPMs).

FIG. 2. Operating principle of a SPAD, the main element of a SiPM microcell. Left: a free charge carrier is generated in the depletion region by an absorbed photon. The electric field E in the depletion region separates the electron and the hole. Right: above the breakdown voltage, the accelerated carrier generates further electron–hole pairs through impact ionization, producing an avalanche of order 105 carriers from a single initial carrier.

FIG. 3. Current drawn by a SiPM as a function of bias volt- age under dim blue LED illumination at 9 mK (the curve is a linear interpolation of the data points). In the gray region, below the breakdown voltage VBD (black dashed line), the current is small and the SiPM is not operating. The blue re- gion indicates the operating range, where the photocurrent is proportional to the incident light. Above VUL (orange dashed line), in the orange region, the current rises sharply until it reaches the compliance limit set on the SMU, resulting in ex- cessive heating and unstable refrigerator operation.

FIG. 4. Photographs of the muon detector and its components. Left: Two plastic scintillators wrapped in ESR film and copper tape. Center: SiPMs mounted to PCBs screwed to a copper bracket. Right: The fully assembled detector, ready to be mounted to the mixing chamber of the dilution refrigerator.

FIG. 5. Experimental setup for the muon rate measurements. The Keithley 2450 SMU biases the SiPMs through the readout box, which also decouples the output signals, and the signals are recorded on the oscilloscope. The detector is mounted on the mixing chamber of the dilution refrigerator, and two external muon detectors are placed below the cryostat. Their signals are recorded together with those of the internal detector to identify quadruple coincidences and confirm that the internal coincidences are caused by muons.
